title: Unique Paths

scenarios.description: Calculating the number of possible paths a warehouse robot can take to reach its destination when it can only move forward or right due to physical constraints.
Determining the number of unique ways a player can traverse a grid-based game level when movement is restricted to specific directions.
Computing the number of different routes to travel from one intersection to another in a city with a rectangular street grid, moving only east or south.

solutions.title: Recursion
solutions.approach: Use recursive exploration to try all possible paths from the starting position to the destination. At each cell, we can move either right or down, and recursively count paths from those positions. The base case is reaching the destination cell.
solutions.explanation: The recursive solution explores all possible paths by making a choice at each position: move right (j+1) or move down (i+1). When we reach the destination cell (m-1, n-1), we've found one valid path and return 1. If we go out of bounds (i >= m or j >= n), that path is invalid and returns 0. The total paths from any position equals the sum of paths from moving right plus paths from moving down. This creates a binary tree of recursion where each path from root to leaf represents one possible route through the grid. While correct, this has exponential time complexity due to recomputing the same positions multiple times.

complexity_explanation.time: At each cell, we make two recursive calls (right and down), creating a binary tree of recursion. The maximum depth is m+n-2 (the path length from (0,0) to (m-1,n-1)). This results in approximately 2^(m+n) recursive calls in the worst case.
complexity_explanation.space: The recursion stack depth is at most m+n-2 (the length of any path from start to end), requiring O(m+n) space.

solutions.why_it_works: This solution works by exhaustively exploring all possible paths through the grid. The key insight is that from any cell (i,j), the number of paths to the destination equals the sum of paths from the cell to the right (i,j+1) and the cell below (i+1,j). The base case handles reaching the destination (return 1) and going out of bounds (return 0). By recursively summing these values, we count all valid paths. However, this approach recomputes the same cell positions many times through different paths, leading to exponential time complexity. This is a classic problem with overlapping subproblems, making it ideal for dynamic programming optimization.

common_mistakes: Using incorrect base case conditions, like checking i > m instead of i >= m.
Not handling the destination cell correctly, checking i == m instead of i == m-1.
Forgetting to check both boundary conditions (i >= m and j >= n).
Trying to optimize by checking bounds before the destination check, which can miss the valid end case.
pro_tips: The order of base case checks matters: check destination before bounds to avoid missing the valid endpoint.
This problem has optimal substructure: solution for (i,j) depends on solutions for (i+1,j) and (i,j+1).
The recursion naturally represents the problem structure: sum of two simpler subproblems.
Understanding this solution is essential before moving to DP optimizations.

solutions.title: Dynamic Programming (Top-Down)
solutions.approach: Add memoization to the recursive solution by caching results for each (i,j) position. This eliminates redundant computations by ensuring each cell is calculated only once.
solutions.explanation: This solution optimizes the recursive approach by adding a 2D memoization array. The memo array stores the number of unique paths from each cell (i,j) to the destination. Before computing dfs(i,j), we check if memo[i][j] has already been calculated (not -1). If so, return the cached value immediately. Otherwise, compute it using the same recursive logic (sum of paths from right and down), store it in memo[i][j], and return it. This transforms the exponential solution into polynomial time by ensuring each of the m×n cells is computed exactly once. The memo array effectively builds a solution bottom-up as recursion unwinds.

complexity_explanation.time: Each of the m×n cells is computed exactly once due to memoization. Each computation does O(1) work (two lookups and one addition). Total time is O(m×n).
complexity_explanation.space: The memo array requires O(m×n) space. The recursion stack depth is O(m+n) in the worst case. Total space is dominated by the memo array at O(m×n).

solutions.why_it_works: Memoization eliminates exponential time by caching results for each cell. The key observation is that the number of paths from cell (i,j) to the destination depends only on (i,j), not on the path taken to reach (i,j). This creates overlapping subproblems - the same cell is reached through many different paths during recursion. By storing the result the first time we compute each cell, all subsequent visits to that cell return the cached value in O(1) time. This preserves the correctness of the recursive logic while achieving polynomial time complexity.

pro_tips: Initializing with -1 is standard practice for memoization when 0 is a valid result.
Top-down DP with memoization often mirrors recursive logic more naturally than bottom-up.

solutions.title: Dynamic Programming (Bottom-Up)
solutions.approach: Build a 2D DP table iteratively from the destination backward to the starting position. Each cell stores the number of unique paths from that cell to the destination. Fill the table using previously computed values.
solutions.explanation: The bottom-up approach builds the solution iteratively without recursion. We create a 2D array dp where dp[i][j] represents the number of unique paths from cell (i,j) to the destination (m-1,n-1). We initialize dp[m-1][n-1] = 1 (already at destination). Then we iterate backward from (m-1,n-1) to (0,0). For each cell, dp[i][j] equals dp[i+1][j] (paths from below) plus dp[i][j+1] (paths from right). The key is using += to add to the existing value at dp[i][j], which starts at 0 except for the destination. The answer is dp[0][0]. This eliminates recursion entirely while maintaining the same time complexity.

complexity_explanation.time: We iterate through all m×n cells once, performing O(1) work per cell (two lookups and one addition). Total time is O(m×n).
complexity_explanation.space: The dp array is of size (m+1)×(n+1), requiring O(m×n) space. No recursion stack is needed.

solutions.why_it_works: Bottom-up DP builds solutions iteratively from base cases. The recurrence relation is: dp[i][j] = dp[i+1][j] + dp[i][j+1]. By iterating backward (from m-1 to 0 for rows, n-1 to 0 for columns), we ensure that when computing dp[i][j], the values dp[i+1][j] and dp[i][j+1] have already been computed. The extra row and column (size m+1 and n+1) with zeros act as boundaries, automatically handling the out-of-bounds cases without explicit checks. The += operator adds to the initial value at dp[i][j], which starts at 0 (or 1 for the destination), elegantly handling the base case.

Using = instead of += when dp[i][j] is the destination (would overwrite the 1).
Forgetting to initialize dp[m-1][n-1] = 1.
pro_tips: The extra row and column eliminate the need for boundary checks, simplifying the code.

Bottom-up DP is generally more space-efficient in practice (no recursion stack).
The iteration order (backward) is crucial for correctness.

solutions.title: Dynamic Programming (Space Optimized)
solutions.approach: Optimize space by observing that we only need two rows at a time: the current row and the previous row (row below). Use two 1D arrays that alternate, reducing space from O(m×n) to O(n).
solutions.explanation: This solution optimizes space by noticing that dp[i][j] only depends on dp[i+1][j] (from the row below) and dp[i][j+1] (from the same row to the right). We maintain two 1D arrays: row (representing the row below) and newRow (current row being computed). We initialize row with all 1s (last row has 1 path to destination from each cell). For each row from m-2 down to 0, we create newRow initialized with all 1s (rightmost column has 1 path). Then we iterate from n-2 to 0, computing newRow[j] = newRow[j+1] + row[j]. After processing a row, we update row = newRow. The answer is row[0]. This reduces space from O(m×n) to O(n).

complexity_explanation.space: We use two 1D arrays of size n (row and newRow), requiring O(n) space total. This is a significant improvement over O(m×n).

solutions.why_it_works: This optimization works because each cell in the DP table depends only on the cell to its right (same row) and the cell below (next row). By maintaining just two rows (current and previous), we can compute the same values as the 2D approach. The initialization of newRow with all 1s represents that the rightmost column always has 1 path (can only go down). The iteration backward through columns ensures we use newRow[j+1] after it's computed. Updating row = newRow makes the current row become the previous row for the next iteration. This preserves correctness while significantly reducing space.

solutions.title: Dynamic Programming (Optimal)
solutions.approach: Further optimize space by using a single 1D array. Update the array in-place from right to left, so each cell uses the already-updated value to its right and the old value at its own position (representing the cell below).
solutions.explanation: This is the most space-efficient DP solution using a single 1D array. We initialize dp with all 1s (representing the last row where each cell has 1 path to destination). We iterate through rows from m-2 down to 0. For each row, we iterate through columns from n-2 down to 0, updating dp[j] += dp[j+1]. This works because dp[j] currently holds the value from the row below, and dp[j+1] was just updated to hold the value for the current row at column j+1. By updating in-place from right to left, we avoid overwriting values we still need. The answer is dp[0]. This achieves O(n) space, which is optimal for this approach.

solutions.why_it_works: This solution uses the key insight that dp[j] += dp[j+1] works because: before the update, dp[j] contains the value from the row below (what we need), and dp[j+1] was just updated to contain the value for the current row to the right (what we need). By iterating right-to-left, we ensure dp[j+1] is updated before we use it for dp[j]. The initial dp array represents the last row (all 1s). As we process each row backward, dp transforms to represent that row. After processing all rows, dp represents the first row, with dp[0] being the answer. This elegant in-place update eliminates the need for two arrays.

pro_tips: This is the most elegant DP solution, requiring minimal code and optimal space.
The += operator is key: it combines the current value (from row below) with dp[j+1] (from current row).

solutions.title: Math
solutions.approach: Use combinatorics to compute the answer directly. The number of unique paths in an m×n grid equals the number of ways to arrange (m-1) down moves and (n-1) right moves, which is C(m+n-2, n-1) or C(m+n-2, m-1). Compute this using iterative multiplication and division.
solutions.explanation: This mathematical solution recognizes that any path from (0,0) to (m-1,n-1) consists of exactly (m-1) down moves and (n-1) right moves, for a total of (m+n-2) moves. The number of unique paths equals the number of ways to choose which (n-1) positions get right moves (or equivalently, which (m-1) positions get down moves). This is the binomial coefficient C(m+n-2, min(m-1,n-1)). We compute this using the formula C(n,k) = n!/(k!×(n-k)!), optimized by iteratively multiplying and dividing to avoid overflow. We swap m and n if necessary to use the smaller value for k, minimizing iterations. This achieves O(min(m,n)) time and O(1) space.

solutions.why_it_works: This solution leverages the mathematical fact that grid paths are equivalent to arranging moves. Any valid path requires exactly (m-1) down moves and (n-1) right moves. The question becomes: in how many ways can we arrange these moves? This is a combinations problem: C(m+n-2, n-1) = (m+n-2)! / ((n-1)! × (m-1)!). To avoid computing large factorials and potential overflow, we compute this iteratively: multiply by consecutive integers from m to m+n-2 (numerator) while dividing by 1 to n-1 (denominator). The order matters: we alternate multiply then divide to keep intermediate values manageable. Swapping ensures we use the smaller dimension, minimizing iterations.

Using floating point arithmetic instead of integer, losing precision.
Off-by-one errors in loop bounds (should be m to m+n-2).
pro_tips: This is the most efficient solution in terms of both time and space.
Alternating multiply and divide prevents overflow for typical constraints.
Swapping to use the smaller dimension (min(m,n)) is a key optimization.
This demonstrates how mathematical insight can dramatically improve algorithmic complexity.
For very large inputs, use modular arithmetic if overflow is still a concern.

followups.question: How would you modify the solution if there were obstacles in certain cells that cannot be traversed?
followups.hint: This is problem 63. Use the same DP approach but set dp[i][j] = 0 for cells with obstacles. The recurrence relation remains the same for non-obstacle cells.

followups.question: What if you needed to find the path itself, not just the count?
followups.hint: Track parent pointers or directions during DP. Backtrack from destination to start following the stored directions.

followups.question: How would you handle a 3D grid where you can move right, down, or forward?
followups.hint: Extend to 3D DP: dp[i][j][k] = dp[i+1][j][k] + dp[i][j+1][k] + dp[i][j][k+1]. Same principles apply in higher dimensions.

notes: This is a fundamental 2-D DP problem demonstrating multiple solution approaches from recursion to optimal space-efficient DP to mathematical combinatorics. The DP solutions (especially solution 5) are most commonly used, while the mathematical solution showcases how domain knowledge can achieve superior complexity. Understanding the progression from recursion to memoization to iterative DP to space-optimized DP is crucial for mastering dynamic programming.
